{"id": "80:8/q03", "question": "Why was attention given to the Quraysh leaders?", "turns_on": "Whether the preference reflected hope for conversions or regard for wealth; Wahidi challenges the latter from the verse's actual description.", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q03/p1", "position": "The Prophet hoped their conversion would benefit them and their people.", "reasons": "Biqai says the Prophet addressed a notable in hope of saving him and his kin; Tabrisi's report says he feared the leaders might scorn a following of blind people and slaves. Jishumi says he was trying to convert Meccan leaders."}, {"id": "80:8/q03/p2", "position": "It was not for their wealth.", "reasons": "Wahidi rejects a wealth motive because the verse describes the other man by striving and fear, not poverty."}, {"id": "80:8/q03/p3", "position": "It was for their wealth.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports this suggestion only to reject it; his objection is that the verse does not call the seeker poor."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q04", "question": "How do the clauses about coming and striving work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the following fear clause is circumstantial or predicative, and, if circumstantial, how it attaches.", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q04/p1", "position": "The striving clause is circumstantial to the subject of 'came'; the following fear clause is another circumstance.", "reasons": "Nahhas says the verbal clauses of verses 8 and 9 can be circumstantial accusatives. Samin specifies that 'while he fears' is a circumstance of the subject of 'striving', nested within the first circumstance; he calls treating it as a second coordinated circumstance weak."}, {"id": "80:8/q04/p2", "position": "The clause in verse 9 can instead be another predicate.", "reasons": "Nahhas offers this as an alternative to treating both verbal clauses as circumstantial."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q05", "question": "What does 'yasʿā' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether saʿy denotes actual brisk movement, active pursuit of religious good, or uses movement to express that pursuit.", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q05/p1", "position": "He eagerly pursues religious good, guidance, or knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, as reported by Wahidi, explain it as seeking God's pleasure and good deeds; Ibn Jawzi reports doing good as one of two views. Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi describe pursuit of good, religion, guidance or knowledge. Tabatabai relates the literal quick movement to remembrance, purification and learning; Ibn Kathir says he sought guidance."}, {"id": "80:8/q05/p2", "position": "He walks or moves briskly toward the Prophet, expressing eagerness to meet him.", "reasons": "Damghani gives quick movement and cites 36:20, 20:20 and 28:20. Ibn Jawzi reports walking as one view; Ibn Atiyya allows walking as well as striving in affairs and religious practice. Ibn Ashur calls it brisk walking used for eagerness and sets it against the self-sufficient man's aversion; Tabatabai gives quick walking as its literal sense. Biqai depicts an urgent approach through the crowd."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q06", "question": "What does the verbal picture of the man's striving emphasize?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q06/p1", "position": "His urgency and eagerness strengthen his claim to the Prophet's attention.", "reasons": "Biqai says the verbal form depicts someone coming urgently for good; pressing through a crowd to reach the Prophet gives him a strong claim. Ibn Ashur says brisk walking conveys eagerness to meet, in contrast to the self-sufficient man's disdain."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q07", "question": "How does this clause contrast with the self-sufficient person of verse 5?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q07/p1", "position": "It completes an opposition: the sincere man comes eagerly and fears God, while the other avoids the call and lacks fear.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the coordination completes the division into opposites and reinforces the opening account (80:1–2, 80:5). Biqai says the wealthy man's failure to come and fear is implied by the seeker's arrival and fear; the contrast cautions against slighting the latter. Islahi contrasts worldly absorption with fear of meeting God."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q08", "question": "What is left implicit in the contrast between the two men?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q08/p1", "position": "It uses ihtibāk: the rich man's opposite is poor, and the seeker's coming and fear imply the other's failure to come and fear.", "reasons": "Biqai gives this reciprocal ellipsis, as does Saʿdi al-Mufti in Bursevi."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q09", "question": "What event prompted this admonition?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q09/p1", "position": "Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted the Prophet while he addressed Quraysh leaders; the Prophet turned back to them and the rebuke was revealed.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports al-Hasan and a group; Tabrisi reports the seeker repeatedly asked to be taught and lists ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, Abu Jahl, al-ʿAbbas, Ubayy and Umayya ibn Khalaf. The reports vary in which leaders they name."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q10", "question": "How did the Prophet treat Ibn Umm Maktum afterward?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports describe his treatment of Ibn Umm Maktum specifically or a broader change toward poor people.", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q10/p1", "position": "He welcomed and honored him, asked about his needs, and appointed him deputy over Medina twice.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabrisi give the two appointments. Jishumi and Tabrisi report that the Prophet greeted him as the man over whom his Lord reproached him and asked what he needed."}, {"id": "80:8/q10/p2", "position": "Thereafter he never frowned at a poor person or sought out a rich person, and the poor were honored in his gathering.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this broader account of his later conduct."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q11", "question": "What later report concerns Ibn Umm Maktum?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q11/p1", "position": "Anas saw him at al-Qadisiyya wearing armor and carrying a black banner.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports Anas's account; Tabrisi reports the same observation from Anas ibn Malik, calling it a black standard."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q12", "question": "What does a report say this rebuke shows about revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q12/p1", "position": "If the Messenger had concealed revelation, he would have concealed this passage.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this saying from Ibn Zayd."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q13", "question": "What conduct does the episode teach toward sincere seekers?", "turns_on": "How far the rebuke is generalized: priority for the receptive seeker, equal warning for all, or the basis of human worth.", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q13/p1", "position": "Give the sincere weak seeker attention and priority over prominent people who lack goodness.", "reasons": "Muqatil describes the admonition to welcome him. Ibn Atiyya applies it to scholars; Bursevi extends it to scholars, judges and rulers. Qushayri calls it a reproach on behalf of the poor. Biqai invokes 18:28 and says visible readiness exceeds speculative benefit from elites; Tabatabai describes neglect of the seeker as the rebuked pattern. Islahi contrasts the indifferent and the receptive."}, {"id": "80:8/q13/p2", "position": "Address warning to everyone without social preference; God guides whom He wills.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir names eminent and weak, rich and poor, masters and slaves, men and women, adults and children."}, {"id": "80:8/q13/p3", "position": "Spiritual worth rests on faith and inner state, not wealth or outward rank.", "reasons": "Bursevi says faith ennobles the socially lowly while unbelief diminishes the esteemed. A reported view honors detached poverty; a hadith warns that favoring the rich by wronging the poor destroys a third of one's religion. Bursevi explains the hadith's taḥāmala as either enduring hardship or treating another unjustly and cites the divine saying about failing to feed or give drink to the hungry and thirsty. Ibn al-Zubayr and the report of a dusty overlooked person likewise stress hidden rank."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q14", "question": "Does the episode's lesson extend beyond its original people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q14/p1", "position": "Yes; it applies to anyone with the same qualities.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya identifies Quraysh's disbelievers and Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum as the immediate parties, then extends the lesson to everyone sharing their qualities."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q15", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from the treatment of the Quraysh chiefs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q15/p1", "position": "The Prophet honored them as manifestations of divine majesty; a higher station sees no human distinction beneath God's absolute reality.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this explanation from some great Sufis."}]}
{"id": "80:8/q16", "question": "How does this episode connect with other Quranic instructions about seekers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:8/q16/p1", "position": "It exemplifies the call to stay with those who seek God and the charge to warn those who fear.", "reasons": "Biqai cites 18:28 for keeping company with those who call on God and also 39:65, 38:88 and 31:18 among related admonitions; he says 18:28 follows the pattern of Ibn Umm Maktum's case. Bursevi calls remaining with such people the higher instruction in 18:28. Biqai applies the description of the warner for those who fear in 79:45 to Ibn Umm Maktum."}]}

{"id": "80:9/q01", "question": "Who is the person described as fearing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:9/q01/p1", "position": "He is Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind seeker who came to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies him as the visitor who came striving in the heat. {"id": "80:9/q03", "question": "What does the seeker fear?", "turns_on": "The verb leaves the feared object unstated; the sources supply God, hostile disbelievers, or a physical hazard.", "positions": [{"id": "80:9/q03/p1", "position": "He fears God.", "reasons": "Muqatil says he fears his Lord; Razi includes concern about failing to attend properly to religious duties. Ibn Kathir links this fear to seeking guidance from the Prophet's teaching. Ibn Ashur says God is the understood, omitted object in scriptural usage. Tabatabai calls such fear a sign of taking the Qur'an's reminder to heart, citing 20:2–3 and 87:10. The Study Quran specifies God and the Day of Judgment. Kashshaf, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi give this alongside other possibilities; Biqai holds all three together."}, {"id": "80:9/q03/p2", "position": "He fears harm from the disbelievers as he comes to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Razi gives this as his second possibility. Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi also report it; Biqai describes the harm as persecution for visiting the Prophet."}, {"id": "80:9/q03/p3", "position": "Being blind and without a guide, he fears stumbling on the road.", "reasons": "Razi gives this as his third possibility. Kashshaf, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi also mention lack of a guide; Nasafi calls such wariness customary for blind people. Biqai includes the road hazard alongside the other fears."}]}
{"id": "80:9/q04", "question": "How does the seeker's coming and fear contrast with the self-sufficient person?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired descriptions require a formal ellipsis by ihtibāk; al-Alusi disputes that need.", "positions": [{"id": "80:9/q04/p1", "position": "The two people form an opposing pair: the seeker comes and fears, while the self-sufficient person does neither.", "reasons": "Biqai contrasts the seeker's arrival and fear with the rich man's failure to come and lack of fear, making favoritism especially pointed. Ibn Ashur says the clause about the comer is coordinated with the self-sufficient person and completes a division by opposites. Corpus Coranicum identifies piety in 80:9 as the positive counterpart to istaghnā in 80:5, noting the antonymy of istaghnā and ittaqā in 92:5–8 and their proximity in 96:7."}, {"id": "80:9/q04/p2", "position": "The contrast works by ihtibāk ellipsis: each side implies qualities stated only on the other side.", "reasons": "Saʿdi al-Mufti, as reported by Bursevi, says the earlier mention of the rich implies the later seeker's poverty, while his coming and fear imply their opposites in the first person. Al-Alusi reports the proposal but says the device is unnecessary in light of his prior explanation."}]}
{"id": "80:9/q05", "question": "Why was attention given to the leaders instead of the seeker?", "turns_on": "Whether their social standing implies a material motive; al-Wahidi says the verse provides no such basis.", "positions": [{"id": "80:9/q05/p1", "position": "The Prophet was trying to win the Quraysh leaders to Islam and feared they would scorn followers who were blind or enslaved.", "reasons": "Jishumi's report describes Ibn Umm Maktum interrupting the effort to convert Meccan leaders. Tabrisi's report names ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, Abu Jahl, al-ʿAbbas, Ubayy and Umayya ibn Khalaf, and says Ibn Umm Maktum repeatedly asked to be taught. It gives the Prophet's concern that the leaders might scorn a following of blind people and slaves. Aʿisha's account in al-Durr also places the Prophet with Quraysh chiefs, including Abu Jahl and ʿUtba."}, {"id": "80:9/q05/p2", "position": "Seeking the leaders' riches is not established as his motive.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi rejects that suggestion because the verse describes the other man's striving and fear, not his poverty."}]}
{"id": "80:9/q06", "question": "Who is reproached for turning away from the fearful seeker?", "turns_on": "Whether the unnamed frowner can be identified as the Prophet from the reported incident despite the lack of an explicit name and the character objection.", "positions": [{"id": "80:9/q06/p1", "position": "The Prophet is addressed and reproached for turning from the seeker.", "reasons": "Muqatil says God admonished him to welcome the fearful visitor rather than attend to the self-sufficient. Qushayri calls the passage a reproach to the Prophet on behalf of the poor. Jishumi, the report in Tabrisi, and Aʿisha's account in al-Durr describe him turning back to the leaders. Tabatabai describes the rebuked pattern as attention to wealthy people who scorn truth while neglecting a seeker of purification. Al-Murtada, quoted by Tabrisi, argues against identifying the Prophet as the subject."}, {"id": "80:9/q06/p2", "position": "The passage does not identify the Prophet as the one who frowned.", "reasons": "Al-Murtada says the text does not name him and that frowning at a believing seeker or preferring the rich to the poor would conflict with his noble character."}]}

Aʿisha's account in al-Durr mentions Abu Jahl and ʿUtba and quotes verses 5–10. {"id": "80:9/q09", "question": "What lesson does the incident teach about attention to people?", "turns_on": "The notes draw complementary lessons about equal warning, honoring poor devotees, and the measure of human worth.", "positions": [{"id": "80:9/q09/p1", "position": "Give the sincere seeker full attention without favoring people for rank or wealth.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the Prophet was told to welcome the one fearing his Lord rather than attend to the self-sufficient. Biqai says the contrast warns against favoring the wealthy and slighting the sincere. Tabatabai says the seeker wants purification and fears God, while the wealthy scorn truth and their purification is disregarded."}, {"id": "80:9/q09/p2", "position": "The passage gives special honor to the poor and to companionship with sincere, detached devotees.", "reasons": "Qushayri sees a reproach on behalf of the poor. He says human creation and the cycle of food prove God's power, making rejection of resurrection astonishing."}, {"id": "80:9/q13/p2", "position": "Abasa pairs with al-Naziat through a shared central theme, discourse style, and reasoning, with a distinctive sequence of topics.", "reasons": "Islahi points to 79:45 and says the changed topic order gives this surah its distinctive majesty."}]}
{"id": "80:20/q01", "question": "What does thumma convey here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:20/q01/p1", "position": "It marks a rise in rank, stressing the greater wonder and favor of easing human action through intellect.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says this is a distinction in rank rather than mere temporal delay: intellect is humanity's greatest endowment, and the facilitated path of action follows from it."}]}
{"id": "80:20/q02", "question": "Which path is made easy?", "turns_on": "Whether al-sabīl belongs to the surrounding account of bodily creation and birth, human moral guidance and choice, the path of conduct during life, or each person's divinely decreed course; sources appeal to surrounding verses, 76:3 and 90:10, and accounts of capacity and birth.", "positions": [{"id": "80:20/q02/p1", "position": "The child's passage out of the mother's womb is eased.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and the Kuran Yolu report of his view favor this from the context of creation and bodily change. Al-Qushayrī says the infant emerges headfirst and inverted; al-Ṭabrisī and al-Rāzī describe the turn at delivery and the narrow passage; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Bursawī add the womb's opening; al-Ālūsī adds nerves extending along the passage. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it one of the two passages and connects emergence with the following death and burial. Al-Biqāʿī also extends the route to Paradise or Hell. Iṣlāḥī accepts delivery for mother and child but extends providential easing through nourishment and later activity."}, {"id": "80:20/q02/p2", "position": "God opens and facilitates the ways of good and evil, guidance and error.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and others compare 76:3; al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and others also cite 90:10. Al-Rāzī's Abū Muslim includes worldly and religious choices, enabled by capacity, instruction, reason, prophets and books; al-Ṭabrisī says this enables good and avoidance of evil. Al-Bursawī similarly lists capacity, benefit and harm, reason, prophets and books. Ibn Kathīr calls this the stronger view. Kuran Yolu prefers it as a memorable gift of human choice, distinguishing humans and bringing responsibility. Al-Biqāʿī and Iṣlāḥī include both material and spiritual routes; Iṣlāḥī cites 87:2–3 and 91:7–10. Asad emphasizes intellect and earthly opportunity. The speakers named by individual sources vary, including Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ."}, {"id": "80:20/q02/p3", "position": "The way is the two outcomes of happiness and misery, or felicity and wretchedness.", "reasons": "Reports from Mujāhid express the two alternatives in terms of their outcomes and link them to 76:3, where a person is grateful or ungrateful. Al-Māwardī likewise reports this wording."}, {"id": "80:20/q02/p4", "position": "God eases the particular course or function decreed for each person or created thing.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir and other reports link ease to what God created and decreed for each person. Al-Qurṭubī and Study Quran cite the Prophet's saying that each person is facilitated toward what they were created for; Study Quran broadens the formulation to each thing's function."}, {"id": "80:20/q02/p5", "position": "The path is sound reflection leading to faith, eased by human reason.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports al-Ḥasan; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī instead transmit it from Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, Abū Ṣāliḥ and al-Suddī. {"id": "80:20/q11", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding sequence and the sūra's argument?", "turns_on": "Whether the sequence is read primarily as stages of the body, as divine favors supporting the sūra's warning, or as a recurrent event expressed in the past tense.", "positions": [{"id": "80:20/q11/p1", "position": "It continues the account of bodily creation and birth before death, burial and resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers the birth view because neighboring verses concern creation, bodily development and changing states. {"id": "80:24/q03", "question": "What does reflection on food teach?", "turns_on": "The notes draw distinct lessons from provision, renewed plant life, and the transformation of food into waste; they do not say these lessons exclude each other.", "positions": [{"id": "80:24/q03/p1", "position": "It reveals God's power, care, and human dependence, calling for gratitude and obedience.", "reasons": "Biqai says without divine provision people perish; Tabatabai sees precise, comprehensive planning for human welfare. {"id": "80:24/q04", "question": "What reports illustrate the command to look at food?", "turns_on": "These are distinct reported sayings and episodes, with differing speakers and details, rather than rival versions of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "80:24/q04/p1", "position": "An angel bends a person's neck in the latrine so the person sees what comes out.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim, Mawardi, and Durr transmit this from al-Hasan; the accounts vary slightly between turning and bending the neck."}, {"id": "80:24/q04/p2", "position": "The Prophet asked al-Dahhak what he ate and what it became, making excrement a parable of worldly life.", "reasons": "Tha'labi and Qurtubi transmit the exchange; Qurtubi names al-Dahhak ibn Sufyan al-Kilabi and specifies meat and milk."}, {"id": "80:24/q04/p3", "position": "The Prophet said human food represents the world: however well seasoned, one should consider its eventual end.", "reasons": "Tha'labi transmits the report through Ubayy ibn Ka'b; Qurtubi reports the prophetic statement; Bursevi says it remains true after spices and salt are added. {"id": "80:24/q05", "question": "Why is food singled out rather than drink?", "turns_on": "Whether food is singled out for its richer signs or drink is implicitly included; Alusi rejects the latter explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "80:24/q05/p1", "position": "Food displays more signs of divine power, so drink is left unmentioned.", "reasons": "Alusi offers this as the explanation for the omission."}, {"id": "80:24/q05/p2", "position": "Drink is included under the word food.", "reasons": "Alusi records this explanation but finds it unconvincing."}]}

{"id": "80:24/q07", "question": "How does the call to consider food connect to the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "The notes trace different links: the shift from creation to provision, the force of the preceding rebuke, and the sura's argument for resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "80:24/q07/p1", "position": "The passage turns from human creation and inherent blessings to external provision that sustains life.", "reasons": "Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi Zad follow creation with sustenance; Kashshaf twice describes a shift from blessings in the person to necessities of life. {"id": "80:24/q09", "question": "What does the following water refer to, and why begin the food account with it?", "turns_on": "The notes answer complementary aspects of the following water: its referent and the reason it begins the account.", "positions": [{"id": "80:24/q09/p1", "position": "The poured water is rain from clouds, though the wording can include other waters God brings forth.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives rain as the immediate referent and allows the wider wording; Kashshaf twice identifies the poured water as rain."}, {"id": "80:24/q09/p2", "position": "The account begins with sky and water because they are exalted and water sustains life.", "reasons": "Biqai says this order also recalls first creation and human dependence on the whole world."}]}

{"id": "80:26/q05", "question": "Why is the splitting attributed to God?", "turns_on": "Whether producing or governing a cause warrants attribution of its action, or proper attribution requires the action to subsist in the named agent.", "positions": [{"id": "80:26/q05/p1", "position": "God is the ultimate cause or true creator of the effective causes, so the action can be ascribed to Him figuratively.", "reasons": "Kashshaf attributes either plant openings or plow furrows to God as ultimate cause; Baydawi likewise calls Him their cause.
